title: Asalha Puja
hookLine: the July full moon: the first sermon remembered

cards: A park outside the old city of Benares, the one called Varanasi today. Deer grazing. Five thin, serious men, ascetics who once practiced hard austerities beside him, sitting together.
They see their old companion walking toward them, the one who gave up starving and started eating again. They agree: we won't stand up for him. We won't even greet him.
Then he gets closer, and something in his face makes them stand anyway. What he says next is the first teaching the Buddha ever gave.

teach.b: Asalha Puja. Asalha is the month whose full moon usually falls in July; puja means honoring, an offering.

In Thailand, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, it's the day Theravada Buddhists remember the first sermon, which tradition places two months after the awakening, at the Deer Park at Isipatana, now called Sarnath.
The sermon is called Dhammacakkappavattana: setting the wheel of the dhamma in motion.
It begins with the middle way: not the extreme of chasing pleasure, and not the extreme of torturing yourself, which is exactly what those five men had been doing.

teach.h: THE MIDDLE WAY, THEN FOUR TRUTHS.
teach.b: Then come the four noble truths. In T. W.
Rhys Davids' translation, the first begins: "Now this, O Bhikkhus, is the noble truth concerning suffering."

Birth, aging, sickness, death, being apart from what you love, not getting what you want: dukkha, the unsatisfactoriness of life. The second truth: its arising, in craving. The third: its ending, when craving ends.
The fourth: the path there, the eightfold path. As the Buddha spoke, one of the five, Kondanna, understood; the text says he saw that whatever arises also passes away.
The Buddha exclaimed that Kondanna knew, and he's remembered ever after as Kondanna who knows.
The texts say the gods of the earth cried out that the wheel had been set rolling, and the cry went up through heaven after heaven.
The wheel became a symbol of the teaching, often drawn with eight spokes for the eightfold path.
And a wheel, once set in motion, keeps turning.
Every time someone hears the four truths and understands even a little, it's turning still.

how: On Asalha Puja, Theravada Buddhists visit temples, listen to the first sermon chanted or explained, offer candles and flowers, and many keep the eight precepts.

o: a summer offering to ask the gods for rain
the full moon remembering the Buddha's first sermon
a festival for blessing newly planted rice

games.q: match the piece of the first sermon.
p: the first of the five to understand

s: the five ascetics had agreed not to greet him
they had decided not to stand, and stood anyway as he came near.
the first sermon began with the four noble truths, with nothing before them
it begins with the middle way between two extremes.
Asalha Puja remembers the Buddha's birth
it remembers the first sermon; the birth belongs to Vesak and, in Japan, to April 8.

games.q: you're one of the five ascetics. your old companion, who gave up fasting, walks toward you. you've all agreed to ignore him. what happens?
o: you stand up and greet him anyway.
games.why: the texts say they couldn't keep their agreement: they rose, prepared a seat, and listened to the first sermon.

practice: Say the four truths slowly to yourself, one per breath or two: there is dukkha, the unsatisfactory; it arises with craving; it can end; there is a path.
Then take one small dukkha from today, an irritation, a wanting, and see if you can find the craving in it; just see it, nothing to fix. Rest, the way Kondanna might have rested once he understood.

wordCard.voice: Asalha Puja. The July full moon, when Theravada Buddhists remember the first sermon, the four noble truths, and the wheel of the dhamma set rolling.

orig.note: Pali: the wheel of the dhamma; the first sermon is Dhammacakkappavattana, setting the wheel in motion.

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel still turns. Five men meant to stay seated, and stood. That's day one hundred forty-nine.

sources.tr: Rhys Davids 1881 (Sacred Books of the East XI)
